'''Richard Timothy Durrett''' (born 1951) is an American [[mathematician]] whose research concerns [[probability theory]], [[stochastic processes]], and their applications to [[mathematical biology]], including [[population genetics]], [[ecology]], [[epidemiology]], and [[cancer]] modeling. He is the James B. Duke Emeritus Professor of Mathematics at [[Duke University]], having previously held faculty positions at the [[University of California, Los Angeles]] (UCLA) and [[Cornell University]].

Durrett was elected to the [[United States National Academy of Sciences]] in 2007 and to the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 2002. He is also a fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]], the [[Institute of Mathematical Statistics]], and the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]]. His textbook ''[[Probability: Theory and Examples]]'' was described in a review for the [[Mathematical Association of America]] as one of the two most popular graduate-level texts on probability, alongside [[Patrick Billingsley|Billingsley]]'s ''Probability and Measure''.<ref name="maa-review">{{cite web |last=Rabinovitch |first=Peter |title=Review of ''Probability: Theory and Examples'' by Rick Durrett |website=MAA Reviews, Mathematical Association of America |date=12 January 2011 |url=https://www.maa.org/press/maa-reviews/probability-theory-and-examples |access-date=13 July 2026}}</ref>

== Education ==

Durrett received his Bachelor of Science (1972) and Master of Science (1973) degrees in mathematics from [[Emory University]]. He then entered the [[Operations Research]] program at [[Stanford University]], where he completed his Ph.D. in 1976 under the supervision of [[Donald Iglehart]].<ref name="duke-profile">{{cite web |title=Research and winter weather draws Durrett to Duke |website=Duke Today |publisher=Duke University |date=November 2010 |url=https://today.duke.edu/2010/11/durrett_profile.html |access-date=13 July 2026}}</ref> His doctoral dissertation, titled ''Conditioned Limit Theorems for Some Null Recurrent Markov Processes'', appeared in the ''Annals of Probability'' in 1976.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Durrett |first1=Richard T. |title=Conditioned limit theorems for some null recurrent Markov processes |journal=The Annals of Probability |volume=4 |issue=1 |year=1976 |pages=1–31 |doi=10.1214/aop/1176996177 |issn=0091-1798 }}</ref>

Durrett has said that he initially enrolled at Emory as a [[pre-medical]] student during the [[Vietnam War]] era but switched to mathematics after finding the laboratory component of pre-med unappealing, while still wanting to apply mathematics to real-world problems; this led him to operations research at Stanford.<ref name="duke-profile" />

== Career ==

Durrett began his academic career at the [[University of California, Los Angeles]] (UCLA) in 1976 as an E. R. Hedrick Assistant Professor and was promoted through the ranks to full professor, remaining at UCLA until 1985.<ref name="amacad">{{cite web |title=Richard Timothy Durrett |website=American Academy of Arts and Sciences |url=https://www.amacad.org/person/richard-timothy-durrett |access-date=13 July 2026}}</ref> In 1985 he joined the faculty of [[Cornell University]], where he remained for 25 years.<ref name="amacad" />

In 2010 Durrett moved to [[Duke University]] as the James B. Duke Professor of Mathematics, a position he held until his retirement in 2023, simultaneously serving as associate director of the [[Statistical and Applied Mathematical Sciences Institute]] (SAMSI) in the Research Triangle from 2010.<ref name="duke-profile" /> He was drawn to Duke partly by the milder climate of North Carolina and partly by the opportunities for collaboration with biostatisticians, computational biologists, and applied mathematicians at Duke, the [[University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill]], and [[North Carolina State University]].<ref name="duke-profile" /> Upon retirement he became the James B. Duke Emeritus Professor of Mathematics.

Durrett has supervised more than fifty doctoral students, including [[Rodrigo Bañuelos]] (UCLA, 1984), Claudia Neuhauser (Cornell, 1990), Nathaniel Berestycki (Cornell, 2005), Daniel Remenik (Cornell, 2009), and Shirshendu Chatterjee (Duke, 2011).<ref name="cv"/> He has also mentored postdoctoral fellows including Vlada Limic, Lea Popovic, Soumik Pal, Jon Peterson, David Sivakoff, and Matt Junge.

He served as an editor of the ''[[Annals of Applied Probability]]'' from 1997 to 1999 and has been involved in organizing numerous conferences, including the Southeastern Probability Conference, the Workshop for Women in Probability, and programs at the [[Mathematical Biosciences Institute]] and the [[Banff International Research Station]] (BIRS).<ref name="cv">{{cite web |title=CV for Richard Durrett |website=Duke University |url=https://sites.math.duke.edu/~rtd/CVRDurrett.pdf |access-date=13 July 2026}}</ref>

== Research ==

Durrett's research spans probability theory and its applications. His early work focused on [[interacting particle systems]], [[percolation theory]], and [[contact process]]es, building on the frameworks developed by [[Thomas Liggett|Thomas M. Liggett]] and [[Frank Spitzer]].<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Durrett |first1=R. |title=Oriented percolation in two dimensions |journal=The Annals of Probability |volume=12 |issue=4 |year=1984 |pages=999–1040 |doi=10.1214/aop/1176993160 |issn=0091-1798 }}</ref> His 1980 paper with [[Thomas Liggett|T. M. Liggett]] determined the shape of the limit set in [[Richardson's model]] for the spread of an infection.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Durrett |first1=R. |last2=Liggett |first2=T. M. |title=The shape of the limit set in Richardson's growth model |journal=The Annals of Probability |volume=9 |issue=2 |year=1981 |pages=186–193 |doi=10.1214/aop/1176993462 |issn=0091-1798 }}</ref>

=== Stochastic spatial models in ecology ===

In the late 1980s Durrett began a long-running collaboration with the ecologist [[Simon A. Levin|Simon Levin]] of Princeton University on stochastic spatial models in ecology.<ref name="duke-profile" /> Their 1994 paper ''The Importance of Being Discrete (and Spatial)'' argued that spatial structure can qualitatively change the dynamics of ecological interactions and is among the most cited papers in mathematical ecology.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Durrett |first1=R. |last2=Levin |first2=S. |title=The importance of being discrete (and spatial) |journal=Theoretical Population Biology |volume=46 |issue=3 |year=1994 |pages=363–394 |doi=10.1006/tpbi.1994.1032 |bibcode=1994TPBio..46..363D |issn=0040-5809 }}</ref> Their subsequent papers studied species–area curves, allelopathy, interspecific competition, and the spread of epidemics using interacting particle systems and stochastic spatial models.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Durrett |first1=R. |last2=Levin |first2=S. |title=Spatial aspects of interspecific competition |journal=Theoretical Population Biology |volume=53 |issue=3 |year=1998 |pages=30–43 |doi=10.1006/tpbi.1997.1331 |issn=0040-5809 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Durrett |first1=R. |last2=Levin |first2=S. |title=Stochastic spatial models: a user's guide to ecological applications |journal=Philosophical Transactions of the Royal Society of London. Series B: Biological Sciences |volume=343 |issue=1305 |year=1994 |pages=329–350 |doi=10.1098/rstb.1994.0028 |issn=0962-8436 }}</ref>

=== Population genetics and cancer ===

Beginning in the late 1990s Durrett turned to [[population genetics]], working with [[Chip Aquadro|C. F. Aquadro]] and others on the evolutionary dynamics of microsatellite repeat length distributions<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Kruglyak |first1=S. |last2=Durrett |first2=R. |last3=Schug |first3=M. |last4=Aquadro |first4=C. |title=Equilibrium distributions of microsatellite repeat length resulting from a balance between slippage events and point mutations |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=95 |issue=18 |year=1998 |pages=10774–10778 |doi=10.1073/pnas.95.18.10774 |pmc=27948 |issn=0027-8424 |pmid=9724780 }}</ref> and, with Jason Schweinsberg, on approximating [[selective sweep]]s by random partitions.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Durrett |first1=R. |last2=Schweinsberg |first2=J. |title=Random partitions approximating the coalescence of lineages during a selective sweep |journal=The Annals of Applied Probability |volume=15 |issue=3 |year=2005 |pages=1591–1651 |doi=10.1214/105051605000000329 |issn=1050-5164 }}</ref> His 2008 paper with Deena Schmidt, ''Waiting for two mutations'', studied the limits of Darwinian evolution in regulatory sequence evolution.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Durrett |first1=R. |last2=Schmidt |first2=D. |title=Waiting for two mutations: with applications to regulatory sequence evolution and the limits of Darwinian evolution |journal=Genetics |volume=180 |issue=1 |year=2008 |pages=1501–1509 |doi=10.1534/genetics.107.082971 |pmc=2535691 |issn=0016-6731 |pmid=18791261 }}</ref>

Durrett's later research has applied [[branching process]]es and stochastic models to [[cancer]] biology, including models of tumor heterogeneity, the evolution of resistance to therapy, and the dynamics of clonal expansion.<ref>{{cite book |last1=Durrett |first1=R. |title=Branching Process Models of Cancer |publisher=Springer |series=Mathematical Biosciences Institute Lecture Series |year=2015 |isbn=978-3-319-16064-1 |doi=10.1007/978-3-319-15461-1 }}</ref><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Durrett |first1=R. |last2=Foo |first2=J. |last3=Leder |first3=K. |last4=Mayberry |first4=J. |last5=Michor |first5=F. |title=Intratumor heterogeneity in evolutionary models of tumor progression |journal=Genetics |volume=188 |issue=2 |year=2011 |pages=461–477 |doi=10.1534/genetics.110.125724 |pmc=3175649 |issn=0016-6731 |pmid=21515573 }}</ref>

=== Random graphs ===

A third strand of Durrett's work concerns stochastic processes on [[random graph]]s. He showed, with Shirshendu Chatterjee, that [[contact process]]es on random graphs with [[power-law]] degree distributions have critical value zero—meaning infection can survive for any positive infection rate.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Chatterjee |first1=S. |last2=Durrett |first2=R. |title=Contact processes on random graphs with power law degree distributions have critical value zero |journal=The Annals of Probability |volume=37 |issue=6 |year=2009 |pages=2332–2356 |doi=10.1214/09-AOP471 |issn=0091-1798 }}</ref> His 2010 Inaugural Article as a member of the National Academy of Sciences, published in the ''[[Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences]]'', examined the spread of epidemics and opinions on random graphs.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Durrett |first1=R. |title=Some features of the spread of epidemics and opinions on a random graph |journal=Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences |volume=107 |issue=10 |year=2010 |pages=4491–4498 |doi=10.1073/pnas.0911198107 |pmc=2842029 |issn=0027-8424 |pmid=20160135 |quote=This article is part of the special series of Inaugural Articles by members of the National Academy of Sciences. }}</ref> This work is collected in part in his monograph ''Random Graph Dynamics'' (Cambridge University Press, 2007; second edition Springer, 2025).<ref>{{cite book |last1=Durrett |first1=R. |title=Random Graph Dynamics |publisher=Cambridge University Press |year=2007 |isbn=978-0-521-86656-9 }}</ref>

== Honors and awards ==

Durrett has received a number of honors recognizing his contributions to probability theory and mathematical biology. He was awarded a [[Sloan Research Fellowship|Sloan Research Fellowship]] from the [[Alfred P. Sloan Foundation|Alfred P. Sloan Memorial Foundation]] for 1981–1983, and an [[American Mathematical Society|AMS]] Centennial Fellowship for 1984–1986.<ref name="cv" /> In 1981 he was elected a fellow of the [[Institute of Mathematical Statistics]].<ref name="cv" /> He received a [[Guggenheim Fellowship]] for 1988–1989.<ref name="duke-profile" />

In 1990 he delivered a 45-minute invited lecture at the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] in Kyoto.<ref name="cv" /> He gave the Coxeter Lectures at the [[Fields Institute]] in 1999 and the [[Wald Lectures|IMS Wald Lectures]] at the World Congress of Probability and Statistics in Singapore in 2008.<ref name="cv" />

Durrett was elected to the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]] in 2002<ref name="amacad" /> and to the [[United States National Academy of Sciences]] in 2007.<ref>{{cite web |title=Richard T. Durrett |website=National Academy of Sciences Member Directory |url=http://www.nasonline.org/member-directory/members/2518086.html |access-date=13 July 2026}}</ref> He was elected a fellow of the [[American Association for the Advancement of Science]] in 2009<ref name="cv" /> and was named a fellow of the [[American Mathematical Society]] in the inaugural class of 2012.<ref>{{cite web |title=List of Fellows of the American Mathematical Society |website=American Mathematical Society |url=https://www.ams.org/profession/fellows-list |access-date=13 July 2026}}</ref>
